transcript.text: Samsung RS68A8820S9/EU flashing 22E on the display and the fridge side isn't as cold as it should be. What does 22E mean and can I fix it?

22E is a fridge evaporator-fan error: the appliance is not detecting the fan that circulates cold air for the fridge side. The fan itself may have failed, but it can also be held by ice. Ice build-up is commonly caused by a defrost fault, so it would be premature to buy a fan just from the code. 1. Check the fridge temperature is set around 3–5°C, and make sure food is not covering the air vents at the back/top of the fridge. If a vent is blocked, clear it and allow several hours with the doors mostly shut.
2. Open the freezer and hold its door switch in for 20–30 seconds (the small switch the door presses). Listen for a fan whirr. A silent fan suggests a failed or ice-jammed fan; rattling or scraping points more towards ice.
3. Look for heavy frost or a bulging sheet of ice on the rear wall inside the freezer. That would favour a defrost-system problem choking the airflow, rather than simply a failed fan motor. Switch off and unplug the appliance before attempting to move food, clear ice, or do anything beyond these observations. Do not chip ice with a knife or sharp tool. If the freezer remains cold but the fan is silent and there is no heavy ice, an engineer would normally investigate the evaporator fan and its wiring/control. If there is heavy ice, a full manual defrost may restore cooling temporarily, but a recurring ice-up needs repair of the defrost system.

Fridge is reading 9C and the airflow from the fridge vents is very weak. I get an occasional ticking/scraping sound from the back panel inside the fridge, and there's a bit of frost round the vent at the top back of the fridge. I couldn't tell what the freezer fan was doing or what the freezer back wall looks like. No burning smell and nothing tripping, by the way.

22E is consistent with the fridge evaporator fan not turning, or not being detected turning. With the fridge at 9°C, very weak vent airflow, frost at the vent and a ticking/scraping noise behind the fridge back panel, the leading possibility is that the fan blade is catching ice. A failed fan motor remains possible, but a scrape rather than complete silence makes ice more likely. The most useful next step is a full manual defrost, both as a safe temporary recovery and a diagnostic test:
1. Switch the appliance off and unplug it. Move food to cool bags/another fridge-freezer, put towels down, and leave both doors open for 24–48 hours so hidden ice behind the internal panels can fully melt. Do not chip at ice or use sharp tools.
2. Dry it, switch it back on, and allow several hours with the doors mostly shut. If the airflow becomes strong again, the fan was probably ice-jammed.
3. If it cools properly after defrosting but frost, scraping and 22E return within days or weeks, the underlying fault is likely in the automatic defrost system. That needs an engineer to test the heater, sensor/thermal protection and control circuit. If 22E remains and the fridge airflow is still weak immediately after a thorough defrost, the fridge evaporator fan motor, its wiring, or the control board is more likely. That is also an engineer job rather than a part to buy on the code alone.
Ok, I can do the full defrost. I have a cool box for the food. Is it worth checking warranty first? I bought it 3 years ago from Currys and have the receipt.

Yes — it is worth checking before paying for any repair. With the receipt, contact Samsung and/or Currys first, quote the model, 22E code and the 9°C fridge temperature, and ask whether there is any remaining manufacturer cover, Currys care plan, or goodwill support. At three years old it may be outside the standard guarantee, but it costs nothing to check; keep the receipt and take a photo of the error and temperature reading. A full manual defrost should not prejudice a warranty claim and is sensible because the scraping plus frost makes ice catching the fridge evaporator fan the leading possibility. 22E indicates a fridge fan problem, but it cannot by itself distinguish an ice-jammed fan from a failed fan motor or its control. Do not delay keeping food safe while waiting for a warranty answer: a cool box needs plenty of ice packs and ideally should stay below 5°C. For a 24–48-hour defrost, transfer high-risk chilled food elsewhere if possible. Once it has fully defrosted, dry it, restart it and give it several hours with the doors shut. If airflow returns and 22E clears, the ice blockage was real; if it returns days or weeks later, an engineer needs to investigate the automatic defrost system. If 22E and weak airflow remain straight after the defrost, the fan motor, wiring or control is more likely and needs an engineer.
